Well, the main issues are the archaic/custom software that you tend to find in a business environment and bandwidth concerns. The software itself isn't necessarily insecure, but it's unique enough that it can potentially cause major issues with specific patches. For bandwidth concerns, most networks of any decent size (more than a few workstations) will use a server (ex. WSUS) that delivers patches. This saves a tremendous amount of network usage when every workstation might be using the same patches and policies. The server(s) grab the patches needed by the network, then distribute them in a controlled fashion. Some networks don't delay patches at all or they might wait a few days after the test lab has verified there won't be any problems. They're (in theory) getting patched, but each workstation isn't getting them directly from Microsoft.

That's the biggest reasons that I've dealt with in doing network security for the military.

The catch (as I understand it) is that these free versions of Windows 10 are locked to a particular computer, like the cheap OEM versions of earlier OSes. Once that physical hardware fails or becomes obsolete, that free copy of Windows 10 is gone and you have to purchase a new subscription for your new computer. So it's totally worth it to them to give all existing customers (who would have stuck with their existing OS until their current hardware failed anyway, and hence don't represent any lost income) a free copy of Windows 10, just to take as many non-OEM copies of Windows 7 and Windows 8 out of circulation as possible. Then, a few years down the track, the only Windows OS available is the one you have to pay a subscription for.
